<Conflict due to misinformation — Some sources incorrectly state clams lack eyes, while multiple credible sources describe light-sensitive eyes in some clams>

The retrieved evidence clusters into two opposing positions: several high- and low-credibility sources report that some clams (notably giant clams and ark clams) possess light-sensitive eyes such as pinhole or compound eyes, enabling responses to light changes and motion [d1][d2][d3][d4][d6][d7][d9]. In contrast, multiple sources assert that clams have no eyes at all, which conflicts with the detailed anatomical and behavioral evidence [d8][d11][d12].

d1 and d2 provide detailed, mutually reinforcing descriptions of pinhole eyes in giant clams that detect light and trigger defensive behaviors. d4 and d10 clarify that while most adult bivalves lack eyes, some clams (e.g., ark clams) do have compound eyes. d6 and d7 describe simple ocelli in clams and light-penetrating ocelli in giant clams, respectively. On the other side, d8, d11, and d12 assert clams have no eyes, which contradicts the anatomical and behavioral literature.

Because the query asks a factual biological question, the correct answer must reflect the consensus of the more detailed, evidence-based sources rather than the unsupported claims that clams lack eyes.

Some clams do have eyes. Giant clams possess several hundred small pinhole eyes on the mantle that detect light and movement, enabling rapid defensive responses [d1][d2][d3][d7]. Some clams, such as ark clams, have compound eyes used primarily to detect motion rather than form images [d4][d9]. These findings are consistent with broader molluscan eye diversity, where different bivalve groups evolved distinct eye types [d1][d10]. In contrast, several sources incorrectly state that clams lack eyes entirely, which contradicts anatomical and behavioral evidence [d8][d11][d12].
